newsitem.title: FRANCE: INSTANT VIEW - FRANCE TO REFLECT ON STABILITY PACT.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - FRANCE TO REFLECT ON STABILITY PACT.

text.p: Following are comments from analysts about reports from a meeting of European finance ministers in Luxembourg that France was seeking a period of reflection before a final agreement on the European Union's "stability pact".
SONJA GIBBS, BOND ANALYST, NOMURA INTERNATIONAL
The market has taken this very badly for obvious reasons, everybody was pinning their hopes on the Amsterdam summit but in reality the IGC doesn't finish until the end of June.

The risk is more that the market sees a real conflict between France and Germany - some of the comments coming out from (German finance minister Theo) Waigel sound unfriendly - even though in the longer run it does not mean an end to EMU if there's no stability pact in Amsterdam.

The combined votes of the centre-right and the bulk of the left ought to be able to get the National Assembly to sign off on this. It looks like they are trying to get them to tack on an employment clause. The problem is, it also needs to be sold to the German public. Nobody was expecting an agreement today, it's not the time or the place, it was more a forum for discussion.
The message is that they're struggling to find common ground, and in those circumstances you've got to be looking at unwinding some of those convergence trades.
It's not the end of EMU in itself, but it's not helping.

What we're seeing is the chances of a delay to EMU because of a disagreement between France and Germany increasing. But I think they still both want to see EMU go ahead on time so any fallout should be seen as an opportunity to buy the peripheral markets. The idea of leaving things open until after the Amsterdam summit, and possibly through the summer, is causing some jitters though.

This not a major change, just a restatement of aims. Italian bonds have sold off heavily, but Spain has performed fairly well. Any hint of an EMU delay is bad news for the markets which have converged so rapidly in the last few months, but we are not seeing a delay here. The French have to reinforce their commitment to EMU, which remains quite strong, but also have to keep their commitment to their electorate.
THOMAS MEYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, GOLDMAN SACHS (FRANKFURT)

This is not necessarily contradictory. It shows in the first place that France still feels itself bound to the conditions set down for monetary union and that it still has an interest in introducing the euro on time.

I think the French are playing for time. It would have been far more surprising if a new French government, just a week old and at its very first internationally significant meeting, were to have simply followed the footsteps of their predecessors immediately.
It is a healthy thing to seek time, and a positive sign that they are taking time for reflection. The door is still open for an agreement.
I think the reaction on the markets is exaggerated and hasty.
